Question: A recent law school graduate took and passed the bar examination. Before the swearing-in ceremony, however, the graduate received a letter from the bar examiners indicating that his admission would be delayed until a character fitness investigation had been completed. He was placed in a special drug education program for first- time juvenile offenders and was told that the arrest would be expunged. In addition, the letter provided detailed information about the facts related to the offense. As a result, the examiners hired a special investigator, to look into the matter. As part of the investigator's inquiry, he went to the clerk of the juvenile court where the offense occurred and demanded access to the records concerning the graduate. The clerk refused, citing a state statute that required all court and police records relating to juveniles be sealed. After all other attempts to gain access to the records proved futile, the bar examiners filed suit in federal district court demanding access to the relevant documents. The court should rule that, as applied to this case, the state statute regarding the sealing of juvenile records is

(A) constitutional, because the state has a strong and legitimate interest in rehabilitating juvenile offenders, and this is furthered by protecting them from embarrassment in later life through revelation ofjuvenile offenses.
(B) constitutional, because it safeguards the principle of rehabilitation by shielding individuals from their past juvenile offenses.
(C) unconstitutional, because it infringes on the federal court's jurisdiction over bar admission matters.
(D) constitutional, because juveniles are entitled to the equal protection of the laws.
(E) unconstitutional, because it violates the right of the bar examiners to fully investigate the character of applicants.
(F) constitutional, because it protects the privacy rights of individuals who committed offenses as minors.
(G) unconstitutional, because the bar examiners, as a quasi-judicial agency, is entitled to haveaccess to all relevant public documents.
(H) unconstitutional, because it hinders the interests of justice by preventing the bar examiners from determining the fitness of candidates to practice law.
(I) constitutional, because it promotes the principle of 'forgetting' past juvenile indiscretions to enable successful reintegration into society.
